lead: This unit is about the devices that push information into your eyes, ears and hands: graphics displays, sound displays and haptic devices. After it you can read a display specification, compute angular resolution and stereo depth, and say why a haptic control loop has to run at a kilohertz.
about: A VR system is only as good as what it can make you see, hear and feel. Chapter 3.1 sets the frame: three output channels, and how to choose among them for a task and a budget. Chapters 3.2 to 3.4 walk down the visual chain, from the eye's acuity and depth cues, to personal, head-mounted and large-volume displays, to the stereoscopic methods that create depth. Chapter 3.5 does the same for hearing: the ear, interaural time and level differences, and 3D sound displays. Chapters 3.6 and 3.7 cover the haptic channel, first the devices, then the skin and muscle receptors they must satisfy. Chapter 3.8, taught in only a few universities, closes the loop with haptic rendering, stability and teleoperation.

chapters.idea: A VR system has three output channels, visual, auditory and haptic, and the right device is the cheapest one that meets the task's real numbers.
chapters.depth: Open with the output half of the VR system block diagram: graphics display, sound display, haptic display. Define each in one line. Then the selection criteria, each with its unit: field of view (degrees), angular resolution (pixels per degree), latency and update rate (ms, Hz), stereo or mono, tracking of the head, number of simultaneous users, mobility, hygiene, and cost (rupees). Some syllabi call this chapter choosing output devices for 3D user interfaces; others list it as part of hardware technologies for 3D user interfaces. Show a simple weighted scoring method: list requirements, give each a weight, score each candidate, multiply and add. Mention that the eye and hand are far more demanding than the ear, so visual and haptic choice drives the budget. No deep optics or biology here.

figure.aria: A decision tree that starts from the task and budget and leads to a large-volume display, a head-mounted display, or a stereo monitor with a haptic arm.

chapters.example: A lab has 5,00,000 rupees. Requirements: (a) six students view one walkthrough together, (b) one student does fine stereo work at a desk, (c) one student rehearses a surgical task needing head motion and hand force. Options: stereo monitor 1,50,000 rupees (1 user, no head motion, 1920×1080 total); head-mounted display 3,00,000 rupees (1 user, head motion, 2160×2160 per eye, about 20 pixels per degree); force-feedback arm 2,00,000 rupees; CAVE 40,00,000 rupees. Choose. Answer: (a) needs many viewers, so monitor or CAVE; CAVE is eight times over budget, so drop it. Monitor plus head-mounted display costs 1,50,000 + 3,00,000 = 4,50,000 rupees, inside budget, and covers (a) and (b). Adding the arm gives 6,50,000 rupees, so requirement (c) is deferred to the next year.
chapters.trap: Picking the highest-specification device first, instead of writing the task's numbers and the budget first. Also mixing up input and output devices in the block diagram.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: components of a VR system, the Three I's, VR versus 3D computer graphics.
chapters.leave: The eye and ear themselves, and the internals of each display family, to chapters 3.2 to 3.8.

chapters.idea: The eye is a limited sensor, so displays must be designed around its acuity, its field of view and its depth cues.
chapters.depth: Structure of the eye: cornea, lens, iris, retina, fovea, optic nerve. Rods and cones, their densities and the foveal dip; photopic and scotopic vision. Acuity as the minimum resolvable angle, about 1 arcminute at the fovea, and the conversion to pixels per degree (60 pixels per degree at the limit). Field of view: about 200 degrees horizontally for two eyes, about 120 degrees for binocular overlap, sharp only in the central few degrees; note the role of eye movement. Accommodation and convergence as oculomotor cues, and the well-known conflict in head-mounted displays where the image is focused at a fixed distance but the eyes converge on a different distance. Depth cues: binocular retinal disparity, and monocular cues, occlusion, relative size, linear perspective, shading, texture gradient, motion parallax. Adaptation and after-effects in brief. This underlies stereoscopic display design.

figure.aria: A tree of depth cues split into binocular, monocular and oculomotor groups.

chapters.example: A stereo pair is shown on a screen 2 m from a viewer whose eye separation is 6.5 cm. Find the separation between the left and right images on the screen for an object that must appear (a) 1 m away, (b) 4 m away. Use s = e(D/Z − 1), where s is the on-screen separation in cm, e = 6.5 cm is the eye separation, D = 200 cm is the screen distance and Z is the wanted depth in cm. (a) s = 6.5 × (200/100 − 1) = 6.5 × 1 = 6.5 cm: the images are crossed, left image to the right of the right image. (b) s = 6.5 × (200/400 − 1) = 6.5 × (−0.5) = −3.25 cm: uncrossed, the images sit 3.25 cm apart in the usual order.
chapters.trap: Confusing accommodation (lens focus) with convergence (eyes turning in); they are two different oculomotor cues. Also assuming a bigger screen automatically means sharper vision, when acuity depends on angle, not on size.
chapters.prereq: None beyond school-level optics and biology.
chapters.leave: Stereo hardware and crosstalk to chapter 3.4; head tracking to Unit 2; rendering of depth cues to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Displays are grouped by how much of the viewer's field of view they fill: personal, head-mounted and large-volume, and each family has its own optics and limits.
chapters.depth: Personal graphics displays: desk monitors, stereo monitors, phones held in a viewer; the panel's pixel pitch and the viewer's distance set angular resolution. Head-mounted displays: microdisplay or phone panel, magnifying lens, virtual image at 1 to 3 m as a comfortable focus distance, interpupillary distance adjustment, exit pupil and eye box, weight. Types: opaque (immersive), optical see-through and video see-through (the last two only in outline, since Unit 6 owns AR displays). Large-volume displays: CAVE (four to six projected walls), powerwall, dome, and the fish-tank VR case of a small screen with head tracking. Mention projection geometry, projector blending, and the fact that the CAVE gives a wide field of view but needs a room. Some syllabi call all of this graphics display and split it as personal, head-mounted and large-volume. Use the thin-lens equation 1/f = 1/v − 1/u with the Cartesian sign convention, and magnification m = v/u.

figure.aria: Two light paths, one from a microdisplay through a lens to a magnified virtual image and the eye, and one from the real world through a combiner to the same eye.

chapters.example: A head-mounted display has a lens of focal length 5 cm and its panel 4 cm behind the lens. Find the position of the virtual image, the magnification, and the angle subtended by one 10 micrometre pixel. With 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, u = −4 cm and f = +5 cm, so 1/v = 1/5 − 1/4 = −0.05, giving v = −20 cm: a virtual image 20 cm in front of the lens, 5x magnified. A 10 micrometre pixel appears as 5 × 10 = 50 micrometres at 20 cm, an angle of 50 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.20 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ rad = 0.86 arcminute, just at the eye's acuity limit.
chapters.trap: Quoting the panel's pixel count as if it were resolution. What the eye sees is pixels per degree, and the lens magnification changes it. Also forgetting that the virtual image must sit at a comfortable distance, typically 1 to 3 m, not at 20 cm.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.2 for acuity and field of view.
chapters.leave: Stereo methods to chapter 3.4; optical and video see-through AR displays to Unit 6; rendering to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Stereoscopic displays show each eye a slightly different image, and the resulting disparity is read by the brain as depth.
chapters.depth: The geometry: crossed (front) and uncrossed (behind) disparity, the separation formula s = e(D/Z − 1) with each symbol defined, and the comfort limits (too much disparity, or disparity with wrong accommodation, causes eye strain). Technologies, each with one line on how it works: anaglyph (colour filter glasses), passive polarisation (linear and circular), active shutter glasses time-multiplexed with the display, colour or polarisation multiplexing without glasses (lenticular and parallax barrier, autostereoscopic), and head-mounted displays with two separate panels. Key numbers: refresh rate and per-eye rate, e.g. 120 Hz gives 60 frames per eye per second; ghosting or crosstalk as a percentage; the need to synchronise shutters by infrared or a wired link. Time multiplexing is a timeline, so draw it as one. Keep head tracking out, it is Unit 2.

figure.aria: A timeline showing left and right images shown in turn at 120 Hz, with each eye's shutter open only for its own frame.

chapters.example: A shutter-glasses display refreshes at 120 Hz. Each slot lasts 1/120 s = 8.3 ms, rounded to whole milliseconds in the figure. How many frames per second does each eye receive, and what happens if the panel drops to 60 Hz? At 120 Hz the 120 slots split equally, so each eye gets 60 frames per second. At 60 Hz each eye gets 30 frames per second, which is visibly flickering, so shutter systems need a panel of at least 100 to 120 Hz.
chapters.trap: Swapping crossed and uncrossed disparity, and so putting near objects behind the screen. Also thinking stereo works without correct geometry, or ignoring crosstalk and flicker as exam-worthy limits.
chapters.leave: Head tracking and prediction to Unit 2; AR see-through displays to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The ears locate sound from tiny time and level differences between them, so a sound display must control those cues at each eardrum.
chapters.depth: Structure of the ear: pinna, ear canal, eardrum, ossicles, cochlea, auditory nerve. Range of hearing about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and the cochlea as a frequency analyser. The three localisation cues: interaural time difference (ITD, useful below about 1.5 kHz, maximum about 0.7 ms), interaural level difference (ILD, useful above about 1.5 kHz because the head shadows short waves), and the pinna's direction-dependent filtering, captured as the head-related transfer function (HRTF). Front-back confusion and how small head movements and the pinna resolve it. Sound displays: one loudspeaker, stereo pair, multi-speaker surround, wave field synthesis in one line, and headphones with binaural rendering; cross-talk cancellation for loudspeakers; head tracking and dynamic binaural cues. Latency limits for audio-visual sync, in the tens of milliseconds.

figure.aria: A sound path from source through the head and pinna, splitting into time and level difference cues, then an HRTF filter, headphones and a perceived direction.

chapters.example: A click comes from 30 degrees to the right of straight ahead. The ears are 17.5 cm apart and the speed of sound is 343 m/s. Find the interaural time difference and the delay in samples at 44.1 kHz. Extra path length = 0.175 × sin 30° = 0.175 × 0.5 = 0.0875 m. ITD = 0.0875/343 = 2.55 × 10⁻⁴ s, about 0.26 ms. In samples, 2.55 × 10⁻⁴ × 44100 = 11.2, so about 11 samples. A rendering engine must delay the far ear by 11 samples to place the click at 30 degrees.
chapters.trap: Using ITD for all frequencies. Above about 1.5 kHz the phase difference is ambiguous, and the brain uses level difference and pinna filtering instead. Also forgetting front-back confusion.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for the output channel view.
chapters.leave: Room acoustics and multi-speaker wave field synthesis beyond one line; audio middleware to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A haptic display creates forces or skin deformation on the user, and is classed by whether it pushes the whole limb or only the skin.
chapters.depth: Define haptic display and split it three ways. Force feedback, also called kinesthetic feedback: grounded arm (a pen-like linkage with motors, the Phantom family as an example), exoskeleton worn on the arm or hand, cable-driven systems, and large motion platforms. Tactile feedback: vibrotactile actuators (eccentric rotating mass, linear resonant actuator, piezoelectric), pin arrays, thermal and air-jet displays, and electrotactile in one line. Surface haptics on touchscreens, one paragraph. For each family give the physical quantity it controls (force in newtons, torque in newton-metres, displacement in millimetres, vibration frequency in hertz, amplitude in micrometres), its workspace, its maximum force, and its update rate. Compare with what the hand can sense (chapter 3.7) and with the visual channel: haptics has a small workspace but a very high required loop rate.

figure.aria: A taxonomy of haptic displays split into force feedback devices and tactile devices, with three or four examples under each.

chapters.example: A pen-style force-feedback arm renders a rigid wall with a virtual spring of stiffness k = 1500 N/m. The motors saturate at 3.3 N. Find the force at 2 mm penetration and the deepest penetration that can still be rendered. Force F = kx = 1500 × 0.002 = 3.0 N, which is inside the limit. Saturation penetration is x = F/k = 3.3/1500 = 0.0022 m = 2.2 mm. Beyond 2.2 mm the wall feels soft, because the device can no longer push harder.
chapters.trap: Treating tactile and force feedback as the same thing, and forgetting that the device has a saturation force and a finite workspace. Also quoting motor torque when the question asks for force at the handle.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for the three output channels.
chapters.leave: Receptor physiology to chapter 3.7; control, stability and teleoperation to chapter 3.8; collision detection to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Human haptics is two senses in one: a cutaneous sense in the skin and a kinesthetic sense in muscles and joints, each with its own receptors and limits.
chapters.depth: Skin layers and the four mechanoreceptors with their adaptation and frequency range: SA-I (Merkel, steady pressure, fine edges), RA-I (Meissner, flutter around 5 to 50 Hz), SA-II (Ruffini, skin stretch), RA-II (Pacinian, vibration around 200 to 300 Hz). Density of receptors in the fingertip versus the palm and back. Two-point discrimination threshold, about 2 to 3 mm at the fingertip and much coarser elsewhere, and how it sets the pitch of a pin array. Kinesthetic sense: muscle spindles for length and speed, Golgi tendon organs for force, joint capsule receptors; proprioception and its accuracy (a few degrees at a joint). Force and stiffness discrimination: just-noticeable differences in percent. Adaptation, masking, and the effect of vibration on perceived stiffness. The engineering point: each receptor type tells you which actuator and which frequency band to use.

figure.aria: Two parallel sensory paths, a cutaneous path from skin contact through mechanoreceptors and nerve to cortex, and a kinesthetic path from limb movement through spindles and tendon organs to the cerebellum.

chapters.example: A fingertip pad is covered by a pin array of 1 cm × 1 cm with pins on a 2 mm pitch. How many pins are needed, and is the same array suitable for a palm-sized patch? Along one side there are 10/2 = 5 pins, so the array has 5 × 5 = 25 pins. The fingertip two-point threshold is about 2 to 3 mm, so a 2 mm pitch is at the useful limit. On the palm the threshold is around 10 mm, so the same pitch gives five times more pins than the skin can resolve; a 4 mm or 5 mm pitch would be enough.
chapters.trap: Assuming the skin is equally sensitive everywhere, and confusing the two-point threshold with the resolution of a pin array. Also mixing up which receptor signals vibration and which signals steady pressure.
chapters.leave: Vibrotactile actuator physics to chapter 3.6; perception experiments and human factors to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Haptic rendering is a control loop, and its stability depends on stiffness, loop rate and damping, which is why teleoperation needs force scaling.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. The rendering loop: read position, check collision or use a proxy point, compute force with a spring-damper law F = k(x_wall − x) − bv, send it to the motors, repeat at 1 kHz. Why the loop must be fast: the hand is stiff and fast, so a slow loop feels spongy or unstable. The common stability rule of thumb for a virtual wall, damping b > kT/2 with T the loop period, worked with numbers. Interpolation and force smoothing when the loop is slower than 1 kHz. Teleoperation: master and slave arms, position-position and force-position architectures, force scaling and the effect of communication delay, time-domain passivity only in one line. Say clearly in one line that this chapter completes the subject by joining haptics to control theory.

figure.aria: A closed rendering loop that reads hand position, checks collision, computes a spring force, drives the motors, and returns to reading position on the next cycle.

chapters.example: A virtual wall has stiffness k = 2000 N/m and the loop period is T. Use the rule of thumb b > kT/2, with b in newton-seconds per metre. At T = 1 ms, b > 2000 × 0.001/2 = 1 N·s/m. At T = 10 ms, as on a 100 Hz loop shared with graphics, b > 2000 × 0.01/2 = 10 N·s/m, ten times more damping, which the user feels as thick treacle. This is why haptics runs at 1 kHz while graphics may run at 60 to 90 Hz.
chapters.trap: Thinking a stiffer virtual wall is always better. Stiffness with a slow loop causes buzzing or oscillation, and the fix is a faster loop or more damping, not a bigger spring constant. Also forgetting force scaling in teleoperation.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.6 and 3.7, plus basic control ideas of feedback and stability.
chapters.leave: Collision detection and physics to Unit 4; networking delay and distributed VR beyond one line.
